# Exact weighted simplex inequality for vertex-isolating sections

This proves an all-dimensional extension of the weighted triangle chord
calculation for sections isolating one simplex vertex, and their
complements. In dimensions at least three, it does not include sections
having several vertices strictly on each side.

## 1. The simplex calculation

Let T be a d-simplex, d≥2, and let y be interior, with positive
barycentric coordinates λ_0,...,λ_d. A hyperplane cutting off vertex i
meets its d incident edges at parameters t_j∈(0,1], j≠i. Its section
is a (d−1)-simplex, whose centroid has barycentrics t_j/d at j≠i.
Consequently its section centroid is y exactly when

    t_j=dλ_j,   j≠i.                                    (1)

Such a cap exists exactly when λ_j≤1/d for every j≠i. Its fraction is

    f_i=d^d∏_{j≠i}λ_j.                                  (2)

Use the raw affine margin

    m_i(ξ)=d−Σ_{j≠i} ξ_j/λ_j,

and its continuous gradient u_i. The cap is m_i≥0 and its boundary
passes through y. Moving the margin by a scalar s changes its volume
locally to |T|(d+s)^d∏_{j≠i}λ_j, whenever the section is transverse
to the incident edges. Thus its coarea section mass is |T|f_i.
The identity extends to endpoint cases λ_j=1/d by continuity; the
section remains proper and has a null relative boundary. Equivalently,
the ordinary section mass for a unit normal times that unit normal is
|T|f_i u_i. This vector is unaffected by rescaling the entire margin.

Suppose λ_i≤1/d for every i. Put

    t_i=1−dλ_i≥0,   Σ_i t_i=1,
    D=1−dΣ_i λ_i²=Σ_i λ_i t_i>0.

The gradients u_i have rank d, with their unique linear relation
proportional to (t_i). To check this, a relation Σ_i a_i u_i=0 with
s=Σ_i a_i says that (s−a_j)/λ_j is independent of j, since the only
relation among the barycentric gradients is their sum. Summing gives
a_j=s(1−dλ_j)=s t_j. The converse follows directly.

Therefore the normalized nonnegative section-balanced weights on
vertex-side caps are

    θ_i=λ_i t_i/D.                                      (3)

Their mean fraction is exactly

    F_d(λ)=d^d∏_i λ_i / D
          = ∏_i(1−t_i)/(2 e_2(t)),                      (4)

where e_2(t)=Σ_{i<j}t_i t_j. Zero t_i simply gives zero weight; no
division by t_i occurs in (3).

## 2. A sharp probability-vector product inequality

For m≥2 and a probability vector t=(t_1,...,t_m), define

    R_m(t)=∏_i(1−t_i)/(2e_2(t))

when e_2(t)>0. At a vertex of the probability simplex define R_m=1/2.
This is the continuous extension: writing the dominant coordinate as
1−ε gives numerator ε(1+O(ε)) and denominator 2ε(1+O(ε)), uniformly
over the other coordinates as ε↓0.

**Lemma.**

    ((m−1)/m)^(m−1) ≤ R_m(t) ≤ 1/2.                    (5)

Fix two coordinates a,b, their sum s, and their product p. Let the
other coordinates have sum T=1−s, pair sum E, and complementary
product C=∏_{other}(1−t_i). Then

    R_m=C(1−s+p)/(2(E+sT+p)).

Its derivative with respect to p has the sign of

    E+sT−1+s=E−T²≤0,                                   (6)

because E≤T²/2. Hence replacing a,b by their average, which increases
p, cannot increase R_m. Repeatedly averaging a largest and a smallest
coordinate converges to the uniform vector: the sum of squared
deviations drops by (a−b)²/2, and the largest-smallest gap cannot stay
bounded away from zero. Continuity then gives the lower bound, since
R_m at the uniform vector equals the left side of (5).

Conversely, merging any two positive coordinates into their sum and
zero decreases p, so cannot decrease R_m. Iterate until one coordinate
remains; continuity gives the upper bound 1/2. Degenerate steps with
zero denominator are handled by the continuous extension. For m=2
the ratio is identically 1/2. For m>2 the lower bound is strict away
from the uniform vector: any unequal pair with a positive remaining
sum makes (6) strictly negative; if only two coordinates are positive,
the value is 1/2, strictly above the lower bound.

Taking m=d+1 in (5) proves the exact bounds

    γ_d ≤ F_d(λ) ≤ 1/2.                                 (7)

The lower equality in the interior occurs at λ_i=1/(d+1).

## 3. Reversals, repeated caps, and unavailable vertex caps

If all available vertex cap normals are reversed, the weights are
unchanged and their mean is 1−F_d≥1/2≥γ_d.

More generally, allow both orientations of each available section and
arbitrary nonnegative probability weights, with section-weighted
normal sum zero. Remove equal masses of a cap and its complement;
each removed pair has mean fraction 1/2. The net coefficients on the
remaining raw normals must be a scalar multiple of (t_i/f_i). When
all λ_i≤1/d, their remaining nonzero orientations therefore agree and
have the weights (3), or are all reversed. Every such balanced
combination has mean at least γ_d.

If one λ_k>1/d, the only possible vertex-isolating section is the one
at k, provided every other coordinate is at most 1/d. A balanced family
of these sections must use both orientations of this same plane, with
equal weights, and has mean 1/2. If at least two coordinates exceed
1/d, there are no vertex-isolating sections with centroid y. These
facts describe the limitation of this lemma rather than excluding
multi-vertex sections.

For d=1, a section is a point and the two intervals cut at that point
are complementary. A section-balanced pair has equal weights and
mean 1/2=γ_1 directly; formulas with all λ_i≤1 are consistent with it.
